abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) puts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet, existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that brings this recipe to CaP and turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. Within this harness, we first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, and then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL, however, must credit tens of requests from the agent, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode. Since training runs in simulation, we introduce a physical critic that reads the privileged physical state in simulator, which the policy never sees, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B achieves 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

sections.body: The introduction argues that code-as-policy robot agents are usually built on frontier models or on pre-trained VLA skills, which bound the agent to the data those skills were trained on. Small open VLMs fail in this setting: Qwen3.5-4B solves none of the LIBERO episodes in the authors' harness. The paper proposes CaPtain, an SFT-and-RL pipeline over 22 low-level primitives, with a simulator critic used only during training. Reported results are 55.4% after SFT and 73.8% after RL on held-out LIBERO, and 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX without target-domain training. Stated limits: transfer is limited on RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, with 22.6% and 0.8% success.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing robot code-writing agents rely on frontier models or pre-trained VLA skills, so small open models were never trained end to end.

sections.body: Related work covers code-as-policy agents, end-to-end VLAs and world-action models, and privileged critics. Most code-as-policy systems use frontier models with no weight updates, or orchestrate a frozen VLA as a skill. Few train the code-writing model. CaP-X applies GRPO to a single-turn, text-only 7B coder on three Robosuite tasks, and Guava adds GRPO to Qwen3.5-4B on two MuJoCo tasks. For end-to-end policies, the text reports pi0.5 falling from 97% on standard LIBERO to 12.8% under LIBERO-PRO position and task perturbations, and RIPT-VLA scoring 68.4 against 69.6 for its base OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO-Plus. Privileged critics exist for language models, but none of them reads physical state.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work rarely trains the code-writing model itself, and end-to-end policies drop to 12.8% on LIBERO-PRO perturbations.

sections.body:
CaPtain has three parts.

- **CaPtain-Harness** exposes 22 perception, measurement and guarded-motion capabilities plus finish(). It has no grasp, place or VLA skill, and each call returns a text receipt.
- **Stage 1 (SFT)** trains on synthetic in-harness trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra. The loss covers only tokens the agent produced, and earlier coordinates are replaced by a mask token with probability `0.2`.
- **Stage 2 (RL)** uses a critic that predicts success from 36 privileged features. Each request is credited by the change in predicted success at a fixed request index. Each start state is rolled out `G=4` times.

The critic is removed at test time, and the policy acts from camera images and receipts alone.
sections.heading: CaPtain
sections.headline: CaPtain pairs a 22-primitive harness with SFT on synthetic trajectories and RL using a privileged-state simulator critic.

sections.body: Table 1 reports SFT and RL results on each benchmark, with paired McNemar tests. On held-out LIBERO, RL raises host success from 55.4% to 73.8% (55 episodes gained, 11 lost) and strict success from 52.1% to 67.5%. False finishes fall from 7.1% to 2.1% of episodes, and mean requests per episode fall from 39.1 to 32.6. Gains are +19.0 host points on LIBERO-PRO across three suites, +17.6 on LIBERO-Plus, and +21.2 (Dynamic) and +18.8 (Base) on LIBERO-MAX. All seven LIBERO-Plus dimensions improve at p<0.05. The base Qwen3.5-4B reaches at most 0.3% on any suite.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: CaPtain-4B reaches 73.8% on held-out LIBERO after RL, up from 55.4% after SFT, and keeps its gains under perturbations.

sections.body:
The limitations section lists three constraints.

- **Single-benchmark RL.** RL trains only on the 40 LIBERO tasks with a single 7-DoF arm. Bimanual coordination and tight reach on unfamiliar 6-DoF arms are not addressed.
- **Privileged state.** In an offline study, correlation with the privileged value change falls to 0.49 under 2 cm pose noise, 0.36 under 5 cm, and 0.21 with the policy's own perception. Online RL on hardware would need an external state estimator.
- **Interface coverage.** The action space is bounded by the 22 capabilities and by the behaviors in the synthetic SFT data. Tasks needing sustained force-controlled compliance, such as Wipe, cannot be expressed with guarded Cartesian primitives.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Limits include RL trained only on LIBERO, critic accuracy that falls with pose noise, and no bimanual or force-controlled tasks.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the pipeline: CaPtain-Harness, synthetic SFT trajectories, and multi-turn RL guided by a privileged simulator critic. The authors state that the critic converts sparse episode outcomes into per-request credit, with no privileged information, VLA skills or frontier API calls at test time. They report that CaPtain-4B improves substantially over SFT on held-out LIBERO and three perturbation suites. It matches or surpasses several frontier-model agents at a small fraction of their inference cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen benchmarks and embodiments, and deploys on a physical robot through simulated embodiment adaptation alone. Extending the critic to value termination, bimanual coordination and multi-embodiment workspaces is named as the next step.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: CaPtain turns a 4B vision-language model into a standalone code-as-policy agent that deploys on a physical robot.

sections.body: The appendix covers the policy and harness, including the Qwen3.5-4B policy, the persistent Python tool, and receipt formats. It gives the 22-capability robot API in Table 4 and the RL setup. This includes the 36 privileged features, the critic ensemble of five MLPs, the advantage and returns definitions, and the token-masked policy update. It lists the training distribution of 7,360 start states and the compute used. The main checkpoint is reported at 300 rounds, 75 optimizer updates and 76,800 episodes, at about 1,290 H100-hours derived from wall time. A final table compares CaPtain-4B with published systems across LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-MAX, grouped by type of system.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, the robot API, RL settings, training infrastructure, and per-method comparison tables.
